#9726. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

#9725. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing. #9724. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#9723. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9722. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9721. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9719. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#9718. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

This entry was posted on Wednesday 21st of October 2026 11:26 AM

i discovered this blog two months back from the idscan/Nexus story and was immediately impressed by the journalism on here. as soon as i heard about this doing the rounds elsewhere on social media my first instinct was “i wonder if krebs has written about it yet?” and lo and behold. well anyways, great work as usual, cheers

Maybe I should have kept my blog as pure HTML, perhaps with some perl, instead of going to WordPress.

Just don’t forget the cgi-perl and imagemaps.

Hugo, yes! I finally retired my old Drupal-based site last week and switched to Hugo. For my blog-like site, it’s perfect and saves cost, since it’s served as a static site.

This PHP flaw is a stark reminder of how much of the web runs on shared infrastructure — one critical bug can take government and business sites offline at once. I have been following the patching updates closely, and TrendWire has been a useful source for keeping up with the fast-moving security news around this story. Hopefully hosts patch quickly before mass exploitation ramps up, as the researchers warn.

The vulnerabilities can hardly be referred to as zero-days. They have been known to The PHP Foundation from 2024 but people decided that other bugs were more urgent.

What is fascinating is everyone covering this and sort of ignoring the Indian cert authority issue that made even Krebs hard to POST to days ago. S’okay, timezone and I eligiblegentleman’ed with my cheating billeta hart.

Thanks for the heads-up. I run a small film site on PHP and found out about this from your post, not from my host. If you’re on shared hosting, it’s worth opening a ticket and asking which PHP build they’re actually running instead of trusting the control panel: the version shown there isn’t always the one serving requests.

The scale of this issue makes proactive patch management more important than ever. I’d be interested to see how many affected websites remain unpatched in the weeks following this disclosure.

#9717. Mobile Manipulator Foundations and System Architecture — Ch.11: Performance Metrics [KR]

STATERA Library · Series 03 · Volume 01 · Chapter 11 · KR Source: https://github.com/Statera-Library/03_Vol_01_Mobile_Manipulator_Foundations_and_System_Architecture/blob/main/Chapter_11_Performance_Metrics/Chapter_11_Performance_Metrics_KR.md

이동 성능 지표(Mobility Metrics)는 이동형 매니퓰레이터(Mobile Manipulator)가 운영 환경에서 얼마나 효과적으로 이동하는지를 정량적으로 평가하기 위한 기반을 제공한다. 기존 자율이동로봇(Autonomous Mobile Robot, AMR)과 달리 이동형 매니퓰레이터는 로봇 팔(Robot Arm), 말단장치(End Effector), 가변 적재하중(Variable Payload)을 탑재한 상태에서도 주행 성능을 유지해야 한다. 따라서 이동 성능은 기계 설계(Mechanical Design), 위치 추정 정확도(Localization Accuracy), 운동 제어(Motion Control), 환경 조건(Environmental Conditions), 이동 플랫폼과 매니퓰레이터 사이의 협조 제어(Coordination Control)에 의해 결정된다.

주행 속도(Travel Speed)는 단위 시간당 이동한 거리를 나타내는 기본적인 이동 성능 지표이다. 최고 속도(Maximum Speed)는 이동 플랫폼의 물리적 성능 한계를 나타내며, 정격 운행 속도(Nominal Operating Speed)는 정상적인 운영 조건에서 실제로 사용하는 속도를 의미한다. 평균 임무 속도(Average Mission Speed)에는 가속, 감속, 장애물 회피, 교통 흐름에 따른 지연이 포함된다. 이러한 속도를 구분하여 평가하면 이론적인 이동 성능과 실제 운영 성능 사이의 차이를 명확하게 파악할 수 있다.

가속 및 감속 특성(Acceleration and Deceleration Characteristics)은 이동형 매니퓰레이터가 주행 중 속도를 얼마나 효율적으로 변경할 수 있는지를 결정한다. 빠른 가속은 이동 효율을 높일 수 있지만 진동(Vibration), 바퀴 미끄러짐(Wheel Slip), 로봇 팔의 동적 교란(Dynamic Disturbance)을 유발할 수 있다. 특히 파손되기 쉬운 물체를 운반하거나 작업 위치에 접근할 때는 안정적인 감속이 중요하다. 성능 평가에서는 가속도 제한(Acceleration Limits), 제동 거리(Braking Distance), 운동 평활성(Motion Smoothness), 적재물 안정성(Payload Stability)을 함께 고려해야 한다.

위치 정확도(Positioning Accuracy)는 로봇이 추정하거나 명령받은 위치와 실제 물리적 위치 사이의 차이를 측정한다. 매니퓰레이터가 선반, 기계, 작업대 또는 도킹 인터페이스(Docking Interface)와 상호작용하려면 정확한 위치 결정이 필수적이다. 위치 오차(Positioning Error)는 바퀴 주행거리 추정(Wheel Odometry), 위치 추정 알고리즘(Localization Algorithm), 센서 보정(Sensor Calibration), 환경 변화(Environmental Changes) 등에서 발생할 수 있다. 평가 과정에서는 위치 추정 정확도와 최종 물리적 위치 정확도를 구분해야 한다.

위치 반복정밀도(Positioning Repeatability)는 이동 플랫폼이 반복적인 시험에서 동일한 목표 위치로 얼마나 일관되게 복귀하는지를 나타낸다. 로봇에 일정한 위치 편차(Systematic Positioning Error)가 존재하더라도 반복정밀도가 우수하면 보정(Calibration)이나 국부 위치 수정(Local Correction)을 통해 오차를 보상할 수 있다. 반대로 위치 편차가 불규칙하면 정밀한 로봇 조작이 어려워진다. 반복정밀도는 일반적으로 반복 도킹 시험(Repeated Docking Test)과 위치 편차의 통계적 분석(Statistical Analysis)을 통해 평가한다.

방향 정확도(Orientation Accuracy)는 작은 각도 오차(Angular Error)도 매니퓰레이터의 도달 작업공간(Reachable Workspace)에 상당한 영향을 줄 수 있기 때문에 중요한 이동 성능 지표이다. 이동 로봇이 작업대에 접근할 때 방향이 부정확하면 말단장치의 실제 작업 위치가 달라질 수 있다. 방향 성능은 각도 오차, 방향 반복정밀도(Heading Repeatability), 회전 안정성(Rotational Stability)을 통해 측정할 수 있다. 이러한 측정은 협소한 작업공간과 정밀 조립(Precision Assembly) 작업에서 특히 중요하다.

경로 추종 정확도(Path Tracking Accuracy)는 이동형 매니퓰레이터가 계획된 궤적(Planned Trajectory)을 얼마나 정확하게 따라가는지를 평가한다. 대표적인 측정 항목에는 횡방향 편차(Lateral Deviation), 방향 오차(Heading Error), 최대 추종 오차(Maximum Tracking Error), 평균제곱근 궤적 오차(Root Mean Square Trajectory Error)가 포함된다. 추종 성능은 차량 운동학(Vehicle Kinematics), 제어기 매개변수(Controller Parameters), 위치 추정 품질(Localization Quality), 환경적 교란(Environmental Disturbance)에 영향을 받는다. 정확한 경로 추종은 불필요한 보정 동작을 줄이고 예측 가능한 주행을 지원한다.

자율주행 성공률(Navigation Success Rate)은 사전에 정의된 허용 기준(Acceptance Criteria)에 따라 완료된 주행 임무의 비율을 나타낸다. 성공적인 임무는 일반적으로 충돌, 위험 동작 또는 허용 범위를 초과하는 위치 오차 없이 목표 지점에 도달하는 것을 의미한다. 주행 실패(Navigation Failure)는 위치 추정 손실(Localization Loss), 접근 불가능한 경로(Inaccessible Route), 동적 장애물(Dynamic Obstacle), 제어기 한계(Controller Limitation) 등으로 발생할 수 있다. 성공률은 대표적인 경로, 운영 조건, 임무 지속시간을 고려하여 평가해야 한다.

장애물 회피 성능(Obstacle Avoidance Performance)은 로봇이 운영 환경의 장애물을 감지하고 해석하여 안전하게 우회하는 능력을 측정한다. 주요 지표에는 감지 후 대응 지연시간(Detection-to-Response Latency), 최소 장애물 이격거리(Minimum Obstacle Clearance), 회피 성공률(Avoidance Success Rate), 추가 이동거리(Additional Travel Distance)가 포함된다. 정적 장애물(Static Obstacle)은 통제된 시험 조건을 제공하지만 이동하는 보행자와 차량은 불확실성을 증가시킨다. 시험에서는 장애물 크기, 이동 패턴, 센서 가시성(Sensor Visibility)을 고려해야 한다.

주행 효율(Navigation Efficiency)은 적절한 기준 경로(Reference Route)와 비교하여 로봇이 목표 지점까지 얼마나 효율적으로 이동하는지를 나타낸다. 경로 효율(Path Efficiency)은 기준 경로가 실제로 주행 가능하고 비교 조건이 동일한 경우 기준 경로 길이와 실제 이동거리의 비율로 표현할 수 있다. 과도한 우회는 에너지 소비와 임무 수행시간을 증가시킨다. 그러나 안전 제약(Safety Constraints), 교통 혼잡(Traffic Congestion), 조작 작업 요구사항(Manipulation Requirements)을 고려하면 최단 경로가 반드시 최적 경로는 아니다.

회전 반경(Turning Radius)과 기동성(Maneuverability)은 이동형 매니퓰레이터가 제한된 산업 공간에서 운용될 수 있는지를 결정한다. 차동구동 플랫폼(Differential-Drive Platform)은 자체 중심을 기준으로 거의 제자리 회전이 가능하지만 조향 기반 플랫폼(Steering-Based Platform)은 더 넓은 회전 공간이 필요할 수 있다. 전방향 이동 구조(Omnidirectional Configuration)는 이동 유연성을 높이지만 기계 및 제어 복잡성을 증가시킨다. 기동성 평가에는 통로 폭(Corridor Width), 회전 여유 공간(Turning Clearance), 횡방향 이동 능력(Lateral Motion Capability), 장애물 근접도(Obstacle Proximity)가 포함되어야 한다.

지형 주행 능력(Terrain Traversal Capability)은 이동 플랫폼이 다양한 노면 조건에서 얼마나 효과적으로 작동하는지를 측정한다. 주요 요소에는 최대 등판 경사(Maximum Negotiable Slope), 바닥 단차(Floor Discontinuity), 장애물 극복 높이(Obstacle Crossing Height), 노면 마찰(Surface Friction), 바퀴 접지력(Wheel Traction)이 포함된다. 불균일한 지형은 위치 추정, 적재물 안정성, 매니퓰레이터 보정에 영향을 줄 수 있다. 따라서 시험은 이상적인 실험실 바닥뿐 아니라 실제 배치 환경(Deployment Environment)을 대표해야 한다.

적재하중에 따른 이동 성능(Payload-Dependent Mobility Performance)은 이동형 매니퓰레이터의 질량 분포(Mass Distribution)가 작업 중 지속적으로 변화하기 때문에 중요하다. 적재물 무게(Payload Weight), 로봇 팔의 확장 거리(Arm Extension), 물체 배치(Object Placement)는 무게중심(Center of Gravity), 접지력(Traction), 제동 특성(Braking Behavior), 전복 저항성(Tipping Resistance)에 영향을 준다. 무거운 물체를 팔을 뻗은 상태로 운반하는 로봇은 가속도나 회전 속도를 낮춰야 할 수 있다. 따라서 대표적인 적재 조건과 매니퓰레이터 자세를 포함하여 이동 성능을 시험해야 한다.

운동 안정성(Motion Stability)은 주행 중 발생하는 불필요한 진동, 진동성 운동(Oscillation), 차체 움직임(Body Movement)을 평가한다. 과도한 플랫폼 진동은 센서 측정 품질을 저하시키고 운반 물체를 흔들며 기계적 마모(Mechanical Wear)를 증가시킬 수 있다. 안정성 측정에는 선형 가속도(Linear Acceleration), 각속도(Angular Velocity), 진동 진폭(Vibration Amplitude), 안정화 시간(Settling Time)이 포함된다. 이러한 지표는 정밀 부품을 운반하거나 주행 직후 정밀 작업을 수행하는 이동형 매니퓰레이터에서 특히 중요하다.

도킹 정확도(Docking Accuracy)는 이동형 매니퓰레이터가 지정된 작업대나 인터페이스에 접근하여 정렬하는 능력을 측정한다. 성공적인 도킹에는 종방향(Longitudinal), 횡방향(Lateral), 각도 방향(Angular)의 정밀한 위치 결정이 필요할 수 있다. 기계적 가이드(Mechanical Guide), 시각 마커(Visual Marker), 레이저 기반 위치 추정(Laser Localization), 국부 보정 알고리즘(Local Correction Algorithm)은 정렬 정확도를 향상시킨다. 평가에는 도킹 성공률(Docking Success Rate), 최종 자세 오차(Final Pose Error), 도킹 시간(Docking Duration), 보정 동작 횟수(Number of Corrective Movements)가 포함되어야 한다.

위치 추정 강건성(Localization Robustness)은 변화하는 환경 조건에서도 신뢰할 수 있는 위치 추정을 유지하는 능력을 나타낸다. 산업 시설에는 반사 표면(Reflective Surface), 반복 구조(Repetitive Structure), 임시 장애물(Temporary Obstacle), 시각적 특징이 부족한 영역(Low-Feature Area)이 존재할 수 있다. 이러한 조건은 라이다(LiDAR), 카메라(Camera), 주행거리 추정(Odometry) 기반 위치 추정 성능을 저하시킬 수 있다. 강건성 시험에서는 위치 추정 실패, 복구 시간(Recovery Time), 자세 추정 불확실성(Pose Estimation Uncertainty), 환경 변화에 따른 성능을 평가해야 한다.

복구 성능(Recovery Performance)은 이동형 매니퓰레이터가 예상하지 못한 상황에 직면한 후 주행을 얼마나 효과적으로 재개하는지를 평가한다. 복구 상황에는 경로 차단(Blocked Route), 일시적인 위치 추정 실패(Temporary Localization Failure), 비상 정지(Emergency Stop), 통신 중단(Communication Interruption)이 포함될 수 있다. 주요 지표에는 복구 성공률(Recovery Success Rate), 평균 복구 시간(Average Recovery Duration), 작업자 개입 빈도(Human Intervention Frequency)가 있다. 효과적인 복구 기능은 안전성을 저해하거나 예측 불가능한 움직임을 발생시키지 않으면서 운영 연속성을 향상시킨다.

이동 에너지 효율(Mobility Energy Efficiency)은 대표적인 운영 조건에서 로봇을 이동시키는 데 필요한 전기 에너지를 나타낸다. 에너지 소비(Energy Consumption)는 이동거리, 속도, 가속도, 적재물 질량, 지형, 구동계 효율(Drive System Efficiency)에 따라 달라진다. 킬로미터당 와트시(Watt-hours per Kilometer)와 같은 측정값은 이동 플랫폼 구조 사이의 비교를 지원한다. 이동형 매니퓰레이터에서는 추진 에너지(Propulsion Energy)를 매니퓰레이터, 인지 시스템(Perception System), 컴퓨팅(Computing), 보조장치(Auxiliary System)의 전력 소비와 구분해야 한다.

임무 이동시간(Mission Travel Time)은 출발 지점에서 지정된 목적지에 도착할 때까지 경과한 시간을 측정한다. 정격 속도와 달리 이 지표에는 경로 계획(Path Planning), 장애물 회피, 교통 혼잡, 위치 보정으로 발생하는 실제 지연이 반영된다. 이동시간 분포(Travel Time Distribution)는 평균값만으로 파악하기 어려운 운영 변동성(Operational Variability)을 보여준다. 백분위수 기반 측정(Percentile-Based Measurement)은 로봇이 예측 가능한 생산 일정(Production Schedule)을 충족할 수 있는지 평가하는 데 유용하다.

이동 가용성(Mobility Availability)은 요구되는 운영시간 중 주행 하위 시스템(Navigation Subsystem)이 할당된 이동 작업을 수행할 수 있는 상태로 유지되는 시간의 비율을 나타낸다. 이동 중단(Mobility Interruption)은 구동장치 고장(Drive Fault), 센서 고장(Sensor Failure), 위치 추정 문제(Localization Problem), 제어 시스템 오류(Control System Error) 등으로 발생할 수 있다. 가용성 측정에서는 계획 정비(Planned Maintenance)와 예기치 않은 고장(Unexpected Failure)을 구분해야 한다. 이를 통해 성능 한계가 기계적 신뢰성(Mechanical Reliability), 소프트웨어 강건성(Software Robustness), 운영 절차(Operational Procedure) 중 어디에서 발생하는지 파악할 수 있다.

이동 성능 벤치마킹(Mobility Benchmarking)은 플랫폼 사이의 의미 있는 비교를 위해 표준화된 시험 조건(Standardized Test Conditions)을 필요로 한다. 시험 프로토콜(Test Protocol)에는 적재물 질량, 바닥 특성(Floor Characteristics), 경로 형상(Route Geometry), 장애물 배치(Obstacle Arrangement), 속도 제한(Velocity Limits), 환경 조건을 명시해야 한다. 각 실험은 변동성을 추정할 수 있도록 충분히 반복해야 한다. 평균 성능과 함께 분산 정도(Dispersion), 최악 조건 관측값(Worst-Case Observations), 고장 발생 빈도(Failure Frequency)를 보고하면 이동 성능을 더욱 종합적으로 이해할 수 있다.

실제 환경 이동 성능 평가(Real-World Mobility Evaluation)는 통제된 실험실 측정과 대표적인 운영 현장 시험(Operational Field Trial)을 결합해야 한다. 실험실 시험(Laboratory Testing)은 위치 결정, 경로 추종, 가속, 도킹 성능을 반복 가능한 조건에서 분석하도록 지원한다. 현장 시험(Field Testing)은 보행자, 장비, 교통 혼잡, 변화하는 시설 배치와의 상호작용을 드러낸다. 두 시험 결과를 비교하면 정격 기술 성능(Nominal Technical Performance)과 지속적인 실제 운영에서 달성할 수 있는 성능 사이의 차이를 확인할 수 있다.

이동 성능 지표는 궁극적으로 전체 이동 조작 작업흐름(Mobile Manipulation Workflow) 안에서 해석해야 한다. 높은 주행 속도도 부정확한 도킹으로 로봇 팔 정렬시간(Arm Alignment Time)이 증가하거나 파지 실패(Grasp Failure)가 발생한다면 실질적인 가치가 제한된다. 마찬가지로 뛰어난 위치 정확도를 확보하더라도 과도한 주행 지연이 발생한다면 효율성이 낮아질 수 있다. 효과적인 시스템 평가(System Evaluation)는 이동 성능 측정값을 조작 준비 상태(Manipulation Readiness), 임무 완료(Mission Completion), 안전 제약(Safety Constraints), 전체 작업 성능(Overall Task Performance)과 연계하여 균형 잡힌 공학적 의사결정(Engineering Decision-Making)을 지원해야 한다.

조작 성능 지표(Manipulation Metrics)는 이동형 매니퓰레이터(Mobile Manipulator)가 물체 및 주변 환경과의 물리적 상호작용(Physical Interaction)을 얼마나 효과적으로 수행하는지를 정량적으로 평가하기 위한 체계를 제공한다. 고정형 산업용 로봇(Fixed Industrial Robot)과 달리 이동형 매니퓰레이터는 작업마다 위치 정확도(Positioning Accuracy)와 안정성(Stability)이 달라질 수 있는 이동 플랫폼에서 작동한다. 따라서 조작 성능은 로봇 팔 정밀도(Robotic Arm Precision), 인지 품질(Perception Quality), 파지 안정성(Grasp Stability), 운동 계획(Motion Planning), 힘 제어(Force Control), 이동 플랫폼과의 협조 제어(Coordination Control)에 따라 결정된다.
