When Scientists Admit Mistakes, That Means Science Is Working</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://ggsc.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/images/anthony_fauci_-_abcdef_-_0a21b39134b316e51cdc0dd96c5e6bca3c0093e9-fb_-_abcdef_-_94b15742ccdfc3b16fb1fe35872167fe8d42c35d.webp" alt="When Scientists Admit Mistakes, That Means Science Is Working" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.</p> <p>Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education</p> <p>When the first cases of COVID-19 were discovered in a hospital in Wuhan, I had already studied the U.S. public health response to seven epidemics and pandemics. I am no stranger to the role of politics in pandemic response. Still, the recent Senate hearings grilling Dr. Anthony Fauci alarmed me.</p> <p>Fauci is a physician and immunologist who served as the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and as chief medical advisor to President Trump during the period of Covid-19—who has subsequently become a scapegoat for those who didn’t like the restrictions that came with the pandemic. As Senator Rand Paul put it, based on the evidence-free conspiracy theory that Dr. Fauci funded research that led to the pandemic: “One million Americans died from COVID and not even an apology from Dr. Anthony Fauci.”</p> <p>While we might recognize such claims as preposterous, it would be a mistake to treat these hearings as mere political theater. Those who are treating errors in the understanding of Covid-19 as criminal threaten one of the most important public goods we have during an infectious disease crisis: the willingness of experts to publicly admit mistakes.</p> <p>Dr. Fauci has openly acknowledged missteps, communication errors, and evolving judgments in responding to the COVID-19 pandemic—an honesty that is not matched by his critics. Instead, his honesty has been leveraged by them to sow doubt in science itself.</p> <p>But the reason we turn to experts during a crisis is not because they are omniscient. Of course they aren’t. It is because they learn faster and better than non-experts. Learning, however, is a naturally error-prone process. And learning when a novel infectious disease is fueling a global pandemic is particularly so. One can hope that scientists responding to such a crisis will be able to reduce uncertainties in a linear and predictable fashion. But that is not the norm.</p> <p>As a social scientist, if I discover something new, when I present my findings to my colleagues, the most likely result is that they will tell me all the ways they think I might be wrong. My job is to prove that my findings hold even after considering their counterarguments. Skepticism is essential in the process of separating fact from fiction. We have more confidence in results that have survived such pressure-testing.</p> <p>Experts at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) during the pandemic received just this type of skepticism from other experts. And yet much of the political commentary surrounding these normal and essential controversies cited the evidence of controversy as proof the CDC was flailing.</p> <p>This approach treats science as though the discovery of new facts unfolds like a treasure hunt where the first person to find the treasure opens the lid and everyone can see the treasure with their own eyes. In a treasure hunt, discovery and validation are essentially the same thing.</p> <p>But science does not work this way. Take the discovery of HIV. Dr. Luc Montaignier identified the virus under an electron microscope in February 1983. Uncertainty surrounding whether the virus was causative or opportunistic led to more than a year of additional research, culminating in four papers published by Dr. Robert Gallo and his colleagues in 1984, that affirmed Montaignier’s finding. According to Montaignier, it was one of these publications, in particular, that “convinced the scientific community that this new retrolentivirus was the cause of AIDS.”</p> <p>This example shows something that is true across the sciences. New discoveries that eventually become accepted as scientific facts can linger for an extended period as mere “claims” while uncertainties are addressed.</p> <p>Critics argue that the scientific uncertainty around the discovery of the AIDS virus was unnecessarily prolonged and cost lives. If moving quickly on yet-to-be-validated evidence is the right approach during a pandemic, note that Fauci and his public health colleagues are currently being attacked for doing exactly that. Public health experts believed at the outset that COVID-19 was like SARS, with transmission most likely to occur late in the course of infection. Hence the guidance that directed the public and health care workers to wear masks when caring for patients already showing symptoms. Mounting evidence of asymptomatic infection eventually proved that COVID-19 transmission was very different from SARS, leading to new masking guidance.</p> <p>When should public health experts act on early, but unvalidated, evidence versus taking the time to iron out uncertainties? While it may look obvious in hindsight, there is no magic formula that can sort out in advance when the better course will have been to slow down and validate versus act on plausible, but still uncertain, claims.</p> <p>Climate scientists would almost certainly never argue their experience in the public eye has been a picnic. But they had one big advantage over those trying to guide the response to a pandemic driven by a novel infectious disease. Climate scientists had decades—as opposed to only weeks or days—to conduct research before they were asked to explain what they knew to the public. In fact, climate scientists did not always expect warming to result from burning fossil fuels. Up until the 1950s, the prevailing wisdom was that the oceans would absorb excess carbon dioxide so that there would be minimal if any warming. Roger Revelle and Hans Seuss, who together discovered the error, both received awards for their research.</p> <p>When a novel infectious disease comes to town, the first cases detected are rarely the actual start of the outbreak. There are no tests to make a positive diagnosis. Some of the suspected cases turn out to have other causes. People who are infected are overlooked. Data collected at the outset is patchy and error-prone. As the public health community pivots to emergency response footing, they begin to collect data more systematically. Even so, new data can rapidly overturn early assumptions. The case definition for COVID-19 was updated almost weekly during the first 10 weeks of the pandemic.</p> <p>Monday morning quarterbacking is easy. Try advising countries on how to manage a growing pandemic while the ground is moving beneath your feet.</p> <p>As the United States’ performance during the COVID-19 pandemic is reviewed, even those who are not engaging in political grandstanding tend to reduce the effort to a scorecard that tallies the times experts were right versus the times they were wrong. Even if the reversals are few in number, they are barely tolerated. We usually give examinations to people after they have had time to learn and master the material. What is the right metric to use for public health experts who are trying to inform us when the answers are still being discovered?</p> <p>Speaking of treasure, I think we were lucky during COVID-19 to have public health experts who were willing to admit mistakes as soon as they were discovered. Things will go markedly worse for us if, during the next pandemic, they are less forthcoming.</p> <p>An earlier version of this article first appeared on MS NOW.</p> <p>Ann Keller, Ph.D., is an associate professor of health politics & policy at UC Berkeley School of Public Health.</p> <p>Many decision makers are not drawing from the relevant findings in well-being research. Here's how to change that.</p> <p>When Americans face complex decisions on immigration, climate change or political candidates, they usually don't consider all of the relevant factors.</p> <p>Election season can make many of us feel anxious and helpless. Here are three ways to protect your well-being without tuning out.</p> <p>Do you embrace a diversity of backgrounds and opinions in others?</p> <p>What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.</p> <p>Discover how writing about our ancestors can strengthen our sense of identity, deepen gratitude, and help us find meaning in our own lives.</p> <p>The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.</p> <p>© 2026 The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/scientists_admit_mistakes_science_working_fauci_hearings" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9543"> <h2>#9543. Apple Crisp</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://pinchofyum.com/tachyon/Easy-Apple-Crisp-scaled.jpg" alt="Apple Crisp" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!</p> <p>Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026</p> <p>Made this last night, and it’s now the whole family’s favorite apple crisp. Easy to make and very, very delicious!</p> <p>I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.</p> <p>Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.</p> <p>I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.</p> <p>Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.</p> <p>Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.</p> <p>Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.</p> <p>I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.</p> <p>It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.</p> <p>5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star</p> <p>My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!</p> <p>This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.</p> <p>Keywords: apple crisp, classic apple crisp, apple crisp recipe, fall dessert</p> <p>I love hearing from you! Leave a comment or rating below!</p> <p>I’m Lindsay and I ♡ FOOD. I used to be a teacher, and now making food and writing about it online is my full-time job. I love talking with people about food, and I'm so glad you're here.</p> <p>Did you make a recipe? Tag @pinchofyum on Instagram so we can find you!</p> <p>Your email address will not be published. Required fields are marked *</p> <p>Sign me up for recipes, please!All the food, right to your inbox (and a FREE ecookbook, too!).</p> <p>This looks great- thinking about making for Thanksgiving dessert. How can I prep in advance and bake day of?</p> <p>Can I prep the filling and freeze that so that it’s ready prior to baking day? I need to use these apples but don’t have the space to freeze the whole thing🤦🏼‍♀️</p> <p>This was so good. I made it gluten free by swapping flour for Bob’s Red Mill 1:1 and gluten free rolled oats and it turned out delicious. My new go-to apple crisp!</p> <p>Would gluten free flour work in this recipe?</p> <p>Definitely! We recommend Bob’s Red Mill Gluten-Free 1-1 flour.</p> <p>Looking forward to making this! Can this be prepared ahead of time and then baked right before serving?</p> <p>The apples might leak too much moisture. I would bake ahead of time, then rewarm in a 300 degree F oven.</p> <p>Yeah! Easy, cooked perfect. I used a glass 8×8 dish and it was perfectt, with ice cream 💯👏</p> <p>I’ve made a lot of apple crisps and this one is hands down the best. Crunchy dreamy topping. Only thing I changed was adding ginger and clove to the dough.</p> <p>Made this last weekend and it was incredible. We doubled the crumble topping because that’s the best part and it was so good</p> <p>Can I split this into two small foil pans and cook? Curious if it will equally Make two small pans or I need to make the 9×9 pan.</p> <p>Ok so I’ve been making apple crisp for years. It’s so easy, how can it go wrong. Well I read your post about the apples being “jammy” in this and I could never describe mine like that, so, with an abundance of apples from the orchard and company on the way, I thought why not trying something new? Well, let me tell you, this IS better than my standard recipe! The apples ARE jammy, and it comes together in a delicious way. Company asked for seconds and hubby had it for breakfast. My NEW apple crisp recipe from now on!</p> <p>This. Is. AMAZING! Incredibly easy to prepare and it was a crowd favorite at a recent get together. Pairs perfectly with ice cream. This will be my go-to apple crisp recipe from now on! Thank you for sharing!!</p> <p>This is your cousin 🙂 Made this today with half the sugar and it was so simple and good. Now I have a great smelling house and will come back to this recipe next time.</p> <p>I love sweets but this is just a crazy amount of sugar. If I make this again, I’d likely use 1/3-1/2 of the sugar called for.</p> <p>I have made this twice in the past two weeks and shared the recipe with so many people. It is the perfect fall comfort dessert with a scoop of vanilla ice cream. I love that it is so easy and so delicious and uses ingredients I pretty much always have on hand!</p> <p>Hubby said this is the best apple crisp he has ever had & I have to agree! And trust me that is saying a lot, since this girl would trade almost anything for it at her school lunch. It is so tasty with plenty of topping. 🙂</p> <p>This is the best dessert I have ever made. I made it twice in less than 5 days for different events with friends and everyone loved it! Super easy too!</p> <p>This apple crisp topping is so delicious. This recipe was amazing. We gobbled it up.</p> <p>Comments could not be loaded. Please try again.</p> <p>I'm a former 4th grade teacher, now full time blogger. My husband Bjork and I live in Minnesota. Enter your email and we'll send it right over!</p> <p>Get a Free eCookbook with our top 25 recipes.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://pinchofyum.com/apple-crisp" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9542"> <h2>#9542. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://pinchofyum.com/tachyon/Pastina-Soup-1-scaled.jpg" alt="Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.</p> <p>Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026</p> <p>What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.</p> <p>Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.</p> <p>My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.</p> <p>This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:</p> <p>I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.</p> <p>My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.</p> <p>Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)</p> <p>I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!</p> <p>I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.</p> <p>I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.</p> <p>Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.</p> <p>And then add them right back to the broth pot.</p> <p>Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/glasses-10.jpg" alt="Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.</p> <p>How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.</p> <p>Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.</p> <p>People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.</p> <p>The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.</p> <p>Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.</p> <p>Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.</p> <p>Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.</p> <p>Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.</p> <p>However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.</p> <p>Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.</p> <p>The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.</p> <p>They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.</p> <p>Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.</p> <p>The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.</p> <p>Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.</p> <p>Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.</p> <p>The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.psychiatryadvisor.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2023/09/PSYCH_1000x1000.png" alt="Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”</p> <p>The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.</p> <p>Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.</p> <p>The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.</p> <p>This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.</p> <p>This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.</p> <p>This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor</p> <p>Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832</p> <p>Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.psychiatryadvisor.com/home/topics/addiction/opioid-related-disorder/fentanyl-challenges-current-methadone-induction-protocols/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9538"> <h2>#9538. This Week In Psychology: Patience, Memory And Mental Health (P)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/glass-brain.jpg" alt="This Week In Psychology: Patience, Memory And Mental Health (P)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>The week’s psychology highlights, from patience and success to changing memories, plus emerging studies beyond PsyBlog’s headlines.</p> <p>This week’s roundup brings together highlights from articles published on PsyBlog, alongside other studies in the news worth your attention.</p> <p>Several findings challenge familiar assumptions: patience gives entrepreneurs an advantage, ageing memories gain meaning as they lose detail, and physical activity does not always carry the same benefits for the brain.</p> <p>• Read members-only and premium content • Access courses • Adverts removed • Cancel at any time • 14 day money-back guarantee for new members</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.spring.org.uk/2026/10/this-week-2510.php" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9537"> <h2>#9537. Do You Compare Yourself to Your Partner? It’s Not All Bad</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://ggsc.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/images/couple_partner_comparison_-_abcdef_-_0a21b39134b316e51cdc0dd96c5e6bca3c0093e9-fb_-_abcdef_-_94b15742ccdfc3b16fb1fe35872167fe8d42c35d.webp" alt="Do You Compare Yourself to Your Partner? It’s Not All Bad" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.</p> <p>Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education</p> <p>After venturing through the wasteland of modern dating, it would be natural to harbor disdain for social comparison. Dating apps require you to stand out, which means you can’t just be yourself; you need to sell yourself as more appealing than the 50,000 sexy singles in your area. Putting yourself on display and knowing you’re being compared to others can feel exhausting. But once you’ve swiped right, matched, and established a lasting romantic relationship, surely the social comparisons are all in the rearview mirror…right?</p> <p>That couldn’t be further from the truth. Research suggests we compare ourselves to romantic partners more than anyone else in our lives—on average several times per day. In my own studies, I’ve endeavored to unpack these daily partner comparisons to understand: What kinds of people make partner comparisons, and why? The answer, it seems, depends on the type of comparisons partners are making: either based on our unique abilities, or on the opinions we hold. The good news: Comparisons can offer a learning opportunity and even bring us closer together as partners.</p> <p>Many partner comparisons revolve around who is better at a given activity—also known as “ability-based comparisons.” These comparisons can range from trivial (Who’s the better bowler?) to weighty (Who’s the better parent?).</p> <p>In my latest study with collaborators Robin Edelstein and Stephen Garcia, we studied patterns in who makes more of these ability-based comparisons. We surveyed over 1,100 U.S. adults in romantic relationships, asking them questions about how regularly they compare themselves to their partners. For instance, one question asked them, “To what extent do you pay a lot of attention to how you do things relative to how your significant other does things?” Participants also completed measures of self-esteem, relationship quality, and demographics.</p> <p>The results were clear: People who were younger, those with lower self-esteem, and those in shorter and less satisfying relationships were particularly likely to make ability-based comparisons. Men in relationships with men also reported making more of these comparisons than any other gender pairing, but we only surveyed 37 men in same-gender relationships, so take this finding with a grain of salt.</p> <p>A second type of comparison involves comparing judgments and attitudes—known as “opinion-based comparisons.” In these comparisons, people evaluate their own opinions by comparing with those of their partners. For instance, before enthusiastically locking in a major purchase, a partner might wonder, “Would my partner consider this a good deal, too?” Similar considerations may arise in the contexts of voting, child care, or anywhere judgments lead to decisions.</p> <p>When it came to who was most prone to making opinion-based comparisons, our results flipped: These were most common among people in longer and more satisfying relationships.</p> <p>Taken together, these individual characteristics paint two portraits of people who frequently compare themselves to their partners.</p> <p>The first portrait is that of a young, insecure partner who is in a newer relationship and unsure whether that relationship will work out. Think Bella Swan from Twilight who worries endlessly about whether Edward is too good for her. And, indeed, when we asked participants why they made partner comparisons, two of their motives included assessing equity and predicting the relationship’s trajectory. For instance, participants grappled with questions like, “Am I doing for her as she is doing for me?”</p> <p>The second portrait is that of someone in a long-term relationship who respects the knowledge and expertise of their partner and seeks to harness it as a tool for growth and decision making. For this one, think Leslie Knope from Parks and Rec who regularly compares her own judgments to those of her long-term work wife, Ann Perkins, as a means to make better decisions. This theme, too, emerged from our participants. For instance, one participant lovingly wrote about how his partner outshines him in most areas, and this dynamic continually inspires him to grow.</p> <p>Yet partner comparison isn’t limited to these two portraits. Whereas these portraits describe those who compare most frequently, we found most people make some comparisons sometimes. What motivates occasional comparers?</p> <p>The two most common motives for partner comparison were striving to gain a deeper understanding of oneself and one’s partner. With respect to self-evaluation, one participant shared that they compare regularly to their partner because comparison helps them benchmark their progress toward goals. Want to know if your cooking class has paid off? One of the best ways to evaluate your growth is to see if your latest dish can delight your family in the same way that your partner’s cooking always does.</p> <p>This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.</p> <p>Partner comparisons can also help us understand our partners’ quirks, what we call partner evaluation. For instance, one participant shared how she compares her upbringing to that of her partner, which helps her understand why her partner thinks, feels, and behaves so differently than she does.</p> <p>It’s no secret that social comparison can sting. No parent wants to hear, “I like Mom better,” and no newlywed wants to hear, “How did you land such a catch?” We find in our studies that partner comparisons are often involuntarily thrust upon people who would have preferred not to be compared. It can be true what they say, “Comparison is the thief of joy.”</p> <p>But comparison does more than push our emotional buttons. Partner comparisons help us assess our relationship and calibrate our behavior, such as how we divide household labor. They allow us to make important decisions, like who should take ownership over responsibilities. They serve as sources of growth, and they teach us about ourselves and our partners.</p> <p>Comparing yourself to your partner isn’t necessarily a sign that something’s wrong. Rather, partner comparison can be a handy strategy for making sense of your social world. The key is to use it as a tool that stays in its place, rather than letting it undermine your self-worth or relationship.</p> <p>Serena D’souza contributed to this article.</p> <p>Zachary Reese, Ph.D., is an assistant professor of psychology at the University of San Francisco where he directs the Love and Communication Lab. He received his undergraduate degree in psychology from Goucher College in 2016 and his Ph.D. in social psychology from the University of Michigan in 2022.</p> <p>Sending reels on social media may seem frivolous or distracting, but it actually functions as a form of relationship maintenance.</p> <p>New research is exploring how our brains translate other people's actions into the experience of feeling loved.</p> <p>Our contributors award our annual "Greater Goodies" to the TV shows that might help you be your best self.</p> <p>What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.</p> <p>Discover how writing about our ancestors can strengthen our sense of identity, deepen gratitude, and help us find meaning in our own lives.</p> <p>The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.</p> <p>© 2026 The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/do_you_compare_yourself_to_your_partner_its_not_all_bad" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9536"> <h2>#9536. Fall Freezer Meals #2</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://pinchofyum.com/tachyon/Fall-Freezer-Meals-2-1.jpg" alt="Fall Freezer Meals #2" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>These Fall Freezer Meals have been SO helpful for us. The prep is shockingly easy!</p> <p>Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 14, 2026</p> <p>A few months ago, I discovered what feels like a little life hack.</p> <p>I started spending an hour each month getting a few meals prepped for the month ahead. We’re talking just assembling stuff for my favorite recipes into bags and freezing it!</p> <p>And I can’t tell you how much this system makes me feel like I have my life together! It’s the best.</p> <p>The recipes this month are absolute family favorites for fall!</p> <p>And they all have cook times for Crockpot, Instant Pot, and stovetop methods. 🙂</p> <p>Hope these help make your life easier this month like they have for us!</p> <p>Everything you need is right on them. I print the cards out and attach them to the bags so I don’t have to use my phone at all for the prep or cooking.</p> <p>For the streusel: mix 4 tablespoons melted butter, 1/3 cup brown sugar, and 3/4 cup flour into small crumbles.</p> <p>Spray a muffin tin with avocado oil. Fill tins two-thirds of the way full with batter; top with streusel.</p> <p>Store muffins in an airtight container or bag in the freezer (or fridge). To reheat from frozen, microwave 45-60 seconds.</p> <p>Remove chicken from the sauce and shred. Blend sauce until smooth. Add chicken back in. Serve in tortillas with all the taco fixings you want!</p> <p>Add 1-2 cups heavy cream and 1-2 cups chicken broth (as needed). To thicken: whisk 2 tbsp. cornstarch with 2 tbsp. cold water; add and simmer.</p> <p>Whisk 1 1/2 tbsp. cornstarch in 1 1/2 tbsp. cold water; add to bubbling pot and let simmer until slightly thickened.</p> <p>Stir in 2 cups of fresh spinach and fresh cilantro just before serving.</p> <p>Serve with rice and chili crisp. I also love this with cucumber salad (thinly sliced cucumber and red onion, tossed with vinegar, avocado oil, salt, and sugar).</p> <p>I’m Lindsay and I ♡ FOOD. I used to be a teacher, and now making food and writing about it online is my full-time job. I love talking with people about food, and I'm so glad you're here.</p> <p>Did you make a recipe? Tag @pinchofyum on Instagram so we can find you!</p> <p>Your email address will not be published. Required fields are marked *</p> <p>Sign me up for recipes, please!All the food, right to your inbox (and a FREE ecookbook, too!).</p> <p>I love this idea! Spending just an hour preparing freezer meals for the month sounds like such a practical way to make busy weekdays easier. The variety is great too, especially having options like chicken tinga tacos, wild rice soup, and chickpea curry with different cooking methods. I also appreciate the printable labels and grocery lists because they make meal prep much more organized. These recipes would be especially helpful for anyone balancing a busy schedule with home-cooked meals. Thanks for sharing!</p> <p>Very interesting post. Just thinking about the option to add to instant pot. How would that work? You put everything frozen (without any other unfrozen liquid), put the lid and select the number of minutes? So everything will thaw in the IP before it pressurized?</p> <p>Hi there, how long do these recipes stay good for in the freezer? I would like to have these as back ups. Thank you.</p> <p>Love your recipes! I love curry and the recipe for Chickpea curry looks fabulous, but, my husband is not a chickpea for protein kind of guy. Can I use chicken or shrimp instead and how much would I use?</p> <p>Can you clarify the liquid added to the chicken and wild rice soup? I’m reading 5 cups broth for cooking and then another 2.5 to finish with 2 cups cream, is that right?</p> <p>Hello! Yes, it is another 1-2 cups of broth added, as needed, with the cream. You can adjust depending on how thick you like your soup.</p> <p>Thank you so much for sharing these wonderful ideas! I love your recipes. For the Chicken Wild Rice Soup- Would a combination of Heavy Cream and Whole Milk work here like in the original blog post? What ratio do you think would be best if I did that? Thank you!</p> <p>I love both the original bechamel (butter / flour / milk) method, and the heavy cream method! 🙂 For this version, I opted for the heavy cream just because it’s easier to put onto the small cards. But the bechamel is great and it will get a bit thicker than just using cream. If you want that version, I’d just make the bechamel and add it at the end, using the same quantities as in this post: https://pinchofyum.com/crockpot-chicken-wild-rice-soup</p> <p>Hi there! Always wondering about the prep for chicken thighs, how much do you trim the fat and gristle from them? It takes me so long and I’m always wondering if it’s worth doing.</p> <p>Unless it’s a big piece of fat that you can easily cut off, you can definitely skip the trimming.</p> <p>Love the recipes I have tried! Going to try the freezer prep soup and muffins. Thanks for the recipes</p> <p>Can you use chicken breast instead of chicken thighs in the tinga tacos?</p> <p>Yep! I prefer thighs because they stay a bit juicier, but chicken breasts can absolutely work. 🙂 I would pull them out of the sauce when they’re done and really kind of -chop them into shreddy chunks rather than straight shred them – maybe it’s just me, but I find that sometimes the shredding with chicken breasts can get a bit stringy.</p> <p>Hi Lindsay, Thank you so much for all of your great recipes and ideas! I really appreciate all the hard work.</p> <p>You’re so welcome! I really have enjoyed doing these for myself these last few months, so it’s fun to share them!</p> <p>Lindsay – LOVE your recipes! Question about the freezer meals. There are a couple that you say you freeze the chicken separately but on the Chicken Wild Rice Soup it looks like you put the chicken in the same bag with everything. Can you please clarify for me? Thank you!!</p> <p>Yes! 🙂 Short answer – you can put the chicken in the bag, or add it later. Either can work. Long answer – With the first batch I did in September, I left the chicken out and added it at the time of cooking (and I wrote that into those recipe cards). I liked how it cooked, but I found it was a little bit inconvenient because I didn’t always have chicken on hand when I needed it. So for round two / the set of recipes in this post, I decided to include the chicken in the bag. All these recipes now have chicken going into the bag with everything else, and all the cook times are listed with that in mind.</p> <p>These were so easy and awesome. I prepped one of everything for my friend who just had a major surgery, and another batch for my family. I hope you keep coming out with these!</p> <p>Love that you are sharing these meals with others!</p> <p>Any replacement ideas for chipotles in adobo? Worried too spicy for the kids.</p> <p>Freezer crockpot meals are great for camping. Prep is pretty much done. Put them in the crockpot and enjoy after a day of hiking and fun. Delicious!</p> <p>I’ve been freezer cooking for years and have seen nearly all the websites on the topic.</p> <p>Yours are simply THE BEST label layout I’ve ever come across! Kudos to you!</p> <p>Thank you so much Jerri! I work on these freezer meals with Jenna on our team, and the two of us really try to make them feel as user friendly as possible! 🙂</p> <p>I'm a former 4th grade teacher, now full time blogger. My husband Bjork and I live in Minnesota. Favorite things include my camera, lake days, and dark chocolate.</p> <p>Get a Free eCookbook with our top 25 recipes.</p> <p>The eBook includes our most popular 25 recipes in a beautiful, easy to download format. Enter your email and we'll send it right over!</p> <p>Get a Free eCookbook with our top 25 recipes.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://pinchofyum.com/fall-freezer-meals-2" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/cannabis4-1.jpg" alt="8 Cannabis Risks That Can Follow Young People Into Adulthood (P)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Cannabis can affect the brain and mental health in surprising ways, with some risks appearing particularly concerning for teenagers.</p> <p>Cannabis is often seen as relatively harmless, especially compared with other drugs.</p> <p>But its effects may be particularly important during the teenage years, when the brain is still developing.</p> <p>Recent research suggests that using cannabis at this age may have consequences that last well beyond adolescence.</p> <p>Other studies suggest that negative effects on the brain and mental health may extend across the lifespan.</p> <p>• Read members-only and premium content • Access courses • Adverts removed • Cancel at any time • 14 day money-back guarantee for new members</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.spring.org.uk/2026/10/8-cannabis.php" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9534"> <h2>#9534. Sloppy Joe’s with Ranch Potatoes</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://pinchofyum.com/tachyon/Sloppy-Joes_HighRes-014-scaled.jpg" alt="Sloppy Joe’s with Ranch Potatoes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Easy, saucy, delicious Sloppy Joe’s! My kids’ favorite dinner. Super simple to make with just a few ingredients.</p> <p>Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 28, 2026</p> <p>Here’s the thing – it’s humble, it’s non-fancy, but my husband and my kids are so happy when I make this for dinner.</p> <p>I’ve been on a JOURNEY with these. I tried making Sloppy Joe’s several ways this summer, since my daughter kept asking for them. But with every batch I made, she always kindly let me know that they were still “not as good as the ones at school.”</p> <p>Lucky for me (and all of us), I know several of the wonderful people who do the food service at their school. I was able to get some school recipe intel, which is how I ended up with this very simple “recipe”:</p> <p>It’s rich, and meaty, and easy, and just so very family-friendly.</p> <p>Bjork and I like ours topped with pickled jalapenos or crispy onions, and the girls, of course, like them “plain” on a squishy white bun.</p> <p>I always always make these with what we call Ranch Potatoes, which are the truly the delight of my life. In our house, it’s not Sloppy Joe’s if there’s no pile of crispy, buttery Ranch Potatoes on the side. 🙂</p> <p>Regarding diced onion, pepper, or garlic in the Sloppy Joe filling: this recipe has none. Everyone I cook for enjoys these the same (or even more?) with an uncluttered texture and just a few hits of garlic and onion powder instead, which makes this whole thing even faster and easier.</p> <p>My youngest requested this as her birthday meal this year. Hope you like it as much as we do!</p> <p>Leave it sitting undisturbed for a few minutes so that it develops a nice golden crust.</p> <p>Garlic powder, onion powder, beef bouillon, ketchup, and BBQ sauce!</p> <p>Add some water as needed to make the mixture loosen up and turn a bit glossy. It can just hang out until you’re ready to eat.</p> <p>When you’re close to eating, pop your potatoes in the oven.</p> <p>Once they’re roasty toasty, add a knob of butter and some ranch seasoning. Toss to combine. (If you don’t have ranch seasoning, just use melted butter, fresh garlic, and dill. UNREAL.)</p> <p>Load it onto a soft bun – we love this with ranch potatoes and green beans!</p> <p>5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star</p> <p>Easy, saucy, delicious Sloppy Joe’s! My kids’ favorite dinner. We love these with Ranch Potatoes!</p> <p>White garlic sauce (for dipping, as shown in the video): Whisk 1/4 cup mayo, 1/4 cup plain Greek yogurt, 1 clove grated garlic, 1-2 tablespoons water, and salt to taste.</p> <p>Making Ahead: The meat mixture is ready to go right after you add the ketchup and BBQ sauce, but I usually like to let it simmer for 30-60 minutes to really caramelize around the edges and deepen in both flavor and color. It also works perfectly to keep it warm in the crockpot after cooking!</p> <p>Keywords: sloppy joe’s, sloppy joe sandwiches, easy dinner, kid-friendly dinner</p> <p>I love hearing from you! Leave a comment or rating below!</p> <p>I’m Lindsay and I ♡ FOOD. I used to be a teacher, and now making food and writing about it online is my full-time job. I love talking with people about food, and I'm so glad you're here.</p> <p>Did you make a recipe? Tag @pinchofyum on Instagram so we can find you!</p> <p>Your email address will not be published. I need to add this to my regular rotation. Huge hit with the family!</p> <p>This was a hit with my family. The ranch potatoes are such a smart side with the sloppy joes. I will make this again soon.</p> <p>The sloppy Joes were delicious and easy! I love the idea of adding beef bullion. It definitely made it taste richer. I bought a jar of that for this recipe, along with the gorgeous brioche buns, at Costco. Be prepared to add a little more water at the end. I needed to add more to make it glossy and less sticky. This will be in our regular rotation!</p> <p>Yay – glad you loved in April! I agree about the water, I’m going to update that amount. I often need a bit more as well!</p> <p>My children all ate two helpings. This never happens. And those ranch potatoes are life changing.</p> <p>Amazing! It’s the best feeling! Thanks Lauren! 🙂 🙂</p> <p>This is a simple but delicious and nostalgic recipe. I made this last night and it was a hit.</p> <p>Do you have a favorite BBQ sauce for this recipe? I’m a vegetarian so can’t taste the recipe for my family – would love a recommendation!</p> <p>I’ve used the Trader Joe’s BBQ sauce for the last few batches and I really like it! 🙂</p> <p>Hi Linda! I have used a few kinds! Most frequent ones I’ve used are Trader Joe’s Kansas City BBQ sauce, or Famous Dave’s! 🙂</p> <p>This is such a throwback to the delicious sloppy joes of my childhood, I can already taste them! I’m a vegetarian now- any suggestion of what could be used in place of the meat? Wondering if a combo of beans and mushrooms might work…. off to do some research…. 🙂</p> <p>Hi Gigi: we are also mostly vegetarian (no red meat) so I make tofu crumbles. You can find a recipe on the internet. I freeze my tofu, thaw and drain it and then shred it on the large holes of a grater. Mix with seasonings and bake in the oven. I make a big batch and then seperate them into portions and freeze. Use them for this and anything else calling for ground beef. Hope this helps.</p> <p>Thanks for this! how would you adjust this if you wanted to create this and prep ahead of time, and serve later the next day in a crockpot?</p> <p>Jumping in to add that I also frequently 1.5x or 2x this and freeze whatever we don’t eat, since it works so well as a make-ahead! Especially when I know I’m going to be hosting or serving a crowd. Then I just reheat with a bit more water and sauce or warm in the crockpot.</p> <p>Make as is, then just put on low in a crockpot to rewarm!</p> <p>Ahhhhh Sloppy Joe’s!! My kids are now in their mid-20’s and these are STILL a family favorite haha. I love making them a nostalgic meal when they’re home. Can’t wait to try your version with the beef bouillon base…sounds like a perfect addition!</p> <p>It’s so funny, I make all of this (what I think is) interesting, fun, delicious food, but then I make just regular ol Sloppy Joe’s and my family is just swooning. 🙂 Hope my kids still want me to make these for them when they’re 20!</p> <p>I'm a former 4th grade teacher, now full time blogger. My husband Bjork and I live in Minnesota. How Your Imagination Can Work for You or Against You</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://ggsc.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/images/how_imagination_works_in_the_brain_-_abcdef_-_0a21b39134b316e51cdc0dd96c5e6bca3c0093e9-fb_-_abcdef_-_94b15742ccdfc3b16fb1fe35872167fe8d42c35d.jpg" alt="How Your Imagination Can Work for You or Against You" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.</p> <p>Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education</p> <p>I have a pretty vivid imagination, sometimes for the good, sometimes not. I love it when it helps me to create new stories or songs, or when I can daydream about fun times ahead. But it can also lead to fear or worry, like when I imagine something terrible befalling the people or places I love.</p> <p>Is there some way to nurture the positive aspects of imagination while minimizing the problematic? According to Cassandra Vieten, director of research at the Arthur C. Clarke Center for Human Imagination, there is. In her new book, Imagine That, she explains imagination’s importance in our everyday lives—a way to understand our past, navigate the present, and explore future possibilities. If we learn more about its inner workings, she argues, we can use it more consciously and deliberately to create the kind of life we want.</p> <p>“Imagination is something we all possess, something we can all practice, for free and with equal opportunity,” says Vieten. “When someone develops this capacity, they gain something almost magical: the ability to see multiple futures simultaneously and navigate toward the preferred ones.”</p> <p>Many of us tend to conflate imagination with creativity, thinking that being able to imagine new ideas is the same as bringing them to fruition. While the two may indeed be related, this is far too limited a view of what imagination can be, writes Vieten.</p> <p>“Imagination is an essential, foundational capacity that allows us to simulate reality and transcend it to explore possibilities beyond the known,” she says.</p> <p>In our everyday lives, imagination is what helps us make predictions as well as come up with novel (or creative) ideas. For example, we might imagine how stopping for a coffee on our way to work will help us focus (simulation imagination, based on past experience). But we might also use our imagination to transcend what’s known and come up with a totally new innovation or product idea once we arrive at the office (generative imagination).</p> <p>“Imagination weaves throughout the fabric of our cognitive, sensory, and relational lives—you are constantly speculating, visualizing, rehearsing, wondering,” she writes.</p> <p>These types of imagination show up differently in the brain, writes Vieten. Simulation is primarily centered in the default mode network (DMN), a part of the brain that remains active when we aren’t engaging in a specific task. The DMN is where we tend to mull over future interactions, plans, or options, often subconsciously (or even unconsciously).</p> <p>Generative imagination, on the other hand, comes by freeing ourselves from the DMN’s limitations (or, some would say, tyranny). If we can get out of the everyday chatter and let our minds truly wander freely around disparate parts of the brain, making new neural connections, we have a better chance of generating something truly unique.</p> <p>“Rather than simulating or iterating, comparing and contrasting, generative imagination is focused on combining, reconfiguring, or transcending existing knowledge to generate novel outputs,” writes Vieten.</p> <p>Either way, imagination isn’t frivolous, she writes; it’s important for our everyday functioning as well as creative self-expression. It helps us solve problems, while also expanding possibilities of what could be, giving us “the gift of wonder, whimsy, and surprise, the whoas and the wows of our lives,” she writes.</p> <p>Imagination can sometimes be problematic, though. For example, we might imagine that our spouse is mad at us and worry about what might happen when she gets home from work when, actually, she’s not mad at all. This can cause us needless worry, not to mention potentially trigger a fight.</p> <p>We can also imagine that other people are unpleasant or even dangerous based on untested biases. These can be formed in part via our imagination, which tries to prepare us for unknown encounters, often behind the scenes at an unconscious level.</p> <p>“We regularly imagine entire narratives, scenes, and interactions without intending to or even knowing we’re doing it,” writes Vieten.</p> <p>Our imagination is often busy filling in the missing parts of our memories and perceptions, which are by nature incomplete. Memories, rather than being etched in our minds, are recreated (and often changed) each time they’re recalled. Similarly, we can’t perceive everything at once, so our imagination completes the picture for us, adding interpretations, too. This means it’s easy to corrupt memories or miss details of a situation—which can sometimes lead to problems (think eyewitness accounts of crimes, for example).</p> <p>Understanding these darker sides of imagination can help us tame them somewhat, says Vieten. “You can practice bringing greater attention to what you are imagining, recognize it as imagination, and decide whether it holds useful information, is irrelevant, or is actually causing harm.”</p> <p>While the book covers the neuroscience behind imagination, it’s also about how to harness our imagination more effectively. Your personal imagination style may depend, in part, on your genetics (such as neurodiversity), culture, and life experiences. Understanding this can help you figure out where you might want to try moving the needle one way or the other.</p> <p>To assess your own imaginative strengths and weaknesses, here are some key imagination modes Vieten outlines in her book.</p> <p>1. Receptiveness. “How willing you are to imagine—and how receptive you are to whatever bubbles up.” If you are high in receptivity, you may find it easy to do guided visualizations, for example; if low in receptivity, you may be less willing to imagine unknown scenarios.</p> <p>2. Presence. How much do you embody your imagined experiences? If you tend to be absorbed, immersed, and emotionally involved in imagined scenarios, you’re high in presence; if you tend to observe these imaginings from a distance, you’re less so.</p> <p>3. Embellishment. “How vivid, detailed, and elaborate people make their imaginings.” Those high in embellishment can imagine intricate scenarios with much more detail, clarity, nuance, and complexity. Those low in embellishment might be more “big picture” folks, who may not be able to conjure up details as much.</p> <p>4. Originality. How much your imagination is fueled by what is or could be, based on reality, versus how much it veers from that and is based more on fantasy and novelty.</p> <p>5. Temporality. How much your imagination is associated with time (in other words, assessing the past or projecting into the future) versus how much it is agnostic around time (not based on any particular time). (Vieten admits the science on this mode is not completely settled, but says there appear to be some differences in how people engage with time while imagining.)</p> <p>Each of these modes has pros and cons, she argues. For example, being high in receptivity may mean you’re more cognitively flexible and open to new experiences, but can also mean you’re overly compliant and easily manipulated. Similarly, the upside of being high in originality is that it can fuel advancements in art and science, though it can lead to boredom with everyday life.</p> <p>Considering my own strengths and weaknesses, I noticed that I seem to be high in receptivity and embodiment, but low in embellishment and originality (and mixed when it comes to temporality). Recognizing this makes me think about paying more attention to details in my environment and playing around with more fantastical ideas, especially if I’m wanting to fuel my creativity.</p> <p>To that end, Vieten provides avenues for stretching our imagination in different ways. Some ideas for accessing different aspects of imagination deliberately include rehearsing something before doing it, brainstorming ideas, engaging all of our senses when imagining something, reframing an idea from a different perspective, and freewriting.</p> <p>Vieten also suggests creating environments conducive to being more spontaneously creative. Setting time aside to daydream, being in solitude where your mind can wander, taking walks in the woods to de-stress, or, possibly, taking psychedelic drugs (in a safe, controlled environment) can all help us disengage our DMN and allow creative thoughts to enter more freely.</p> <p>“One of the key ways to make imagination welcome is to remove the practical pressures of the world,” she writes.</p> <p>Imagine That is full of suggestions for unleashing your imagination, all based on the emerging science of imagination that Vieten and her colleagues (and others) are exploring.</p> <p>But while the book reads mostly as a self-help guide, there’s also an important message about why using our imagination is beneficial to society as a whole. Too many of us are experiencing the hopelessness and despair that come with being alive right now, writes Vieten. It’s too easy to get lost in the negative news cycles and focus on all of the problems in the world, making it more difficult to imagine anything better for our collective future.</p> <p>Learning how to engage our imagination more readily can create a sense of hope in our current situation. Not only can it bring more joy and aliveness to our individual lives, countering malaise, it can also lead to new ways of collaborating with others and innovating to solve societal problems, thereby providing a better life for everyone.</p> <p>“So many of the issues facing us locally and globally are rooted in our collective inability to imagine new solutions, alternative futures, creative pathways forward that could build a world that promotes thriving for all,” writes Vieten. “My deepest hope is that [you] take a deeper dive into the science, the practice, and the magic of imagination and [see] how it can re-enchant your life and our world.”</p> <p>Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.</p> <p>A father of three reflects on how becoming a parent taught him about love and helped him grow as a human being.</p> <p>While drug-induced mystical experiences can have benefits, research suggests they may not be enough to create lasting change.</p> <p>Despite how advanced robots have become, getting them to feel the way humans do is an incredibly complex challenge.</p> <p>What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.</p> <p>Discover how writing about our ancestors can strengthen our sense of identity, deepen gratitude, and help us find meaning in our own lives.</p> <p>The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.</p> <p>© 2026 The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_your_imagination_can_work_for_you_or_against_you" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9532"> <h2>#9532. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/talk-negotation-1.jpg" alt="Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.</p> <p>Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.</p> <p>Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.</p> <p>Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.</p> <p>The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.</p> <p>The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.</p> <p>Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.</p> <p>However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.</p> <p>This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.</p> <p>A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.</p> <p>Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.</p> <p>In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.</p> <p>Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.</p> <p>Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.</p> <p>The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.</p> <p>Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.</p> <p>The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.</p> <p>In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.</p> <p>A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.</p> <p>When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.</p> <p>This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.</p> <p>Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.</p> <p>The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.</p> <p>Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.</p> <p>One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.</p> <p>The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.</p> <p>The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.</p> <p>The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.</p> <p>For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.</p> <p>Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.</p> <p>The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004.
